bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 5: Index compression
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition 2009, draft of April 1, 2009)

question: How can the dictionary and the postings lists of an inverted index be compressed so the index uses less disk, fits more in cache and loads faster, without losing information?
contributions: Statistical characterisation of terms (Heaps' law, Zipf's law)
Dictionary compression: fixed-width, dictionary-as-a-string, blocked storage, front coding
Postings compression: gap encoding, variable byte codes, gamma codes, with a Zipf-based size estimate

results.claim: Compressing the postings with gamma codes gives the smallest postings file on Reuters-RCV1, about a quarter of the 32-bit uncompressed size.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); gap-encoded, gamma codes; compared with 400 MB at 32-bit words
results.quote: the actual size of the compressed index is even lower: 101 MB, a bit more than one tenth of the size of the collection

results.claim: Variable byte encoding of the same postings gives 116 MB, a more than 50% reduction against the 250 MB 20-bit index.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); VB with 7-bit payload; versus 250 MB uncompressed (20 bits per docID)
results.note: Against the 400 MB (32-bit) line the reduction is about 71%, and the chapter uses 400 MB for its 'about 25%' ratio on p.104. 116/250 = 46%, so 'more than 50% reduction' holds only against the 20-bit line.
results.quote: the size of the compressed index for Reuters-RCV1 is 116 MB as we verified in an experiment. This is a more than 50% reduction

results.claim: Gamma codes beat VB by about 15% on Reuters-RCV1 but are costlier to decode.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); gamma 101 MB versus VB 116 MB
results.note: Computed from the table: 101/116 = 0.87, so 13% smaller; the text rounds to 15%.
results.quote: γ codes achieve great compression ratios – about 15% better than variable byte codes for Reuters-RCV1.

results.claim: Compression ratio of the compressed index to the uncompressed 32-bit index is about 25%.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); 400 MB (32-bit words) versus 101 MB (gamma) and 116 MB (VB)
results.note: The text prints 'un-compressed' hyphenated in the cache; the quote is normalised by the check if it fails. 101/400=25%, 116/400=29%. The chapter opening says compression ratios of 1:4 'are easy to achieve', cutting storage cost by 75%.
results.quote: The compression ratio for the index in Table 5.6 is about 25%: 400 MB (un-compressed, each posting stored as a 32-bit word) versus 101 MB (γ) and 116 MB (VB).

results.claim: Dictionary stored as a fixed-width array takes 11.2 MB.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); 20 bytes term + 4 bytes document frequency + 4 bytes postings pointer = 28 bytes, times 400,000 terms
results.note: The extracted text prints '11.2megabytes' with no space.

results.claim: Dictionary-as-a-string cuts the dictionary to 7.6 MB, one third smaller.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); 4 bytes freq + 4 bytes postings pointer + 3 bytes term pointer (22 bits) + 8 bytes average term

results.claim: Blocked storage with k=4 gives 7.1 MB.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); one term pointer per block of 4 terms, one length byte per term, saves 5 bytes per block
results.quote: or a total of 400,000 × 1/4 × 5 = 0.5 MB, bringing us down to 7.1 MB.

results.claim: Blocking plus front coding gives 5.9 MB, about half of the fixed-width size.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); front coding saved 1.2 MB 'as we found in an experiment'
results.note: Front coding detail is given only as one experimental figure, 1.2 MB, with no description of the setup beyond Reuters-RCV1.
results.table: Table 5.2, row ~, with blocking & front coding, column size in MB

results.claim: As the block size k grows, the dictionary approaches a floor of 6.8 MB but lookup slows.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); 4+4+1+8 bytes per term, k arbitrarily large

results.claim: Blocking at k=4 costs about 25% more search steps than binary search over the uncompressed eight-term dictionary.
results.setup: Eight-term dictionary of Fig 5.6, each term equally likely as query
results.note: Blocked: (0+1+2+3+4+1+2+3)/8 = 2 steps, '≈25% more'. A toy example, not measured on Reuters.
results.quote: takes on average (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2)/8 ≈1.6 steps

results.claim: Heaps' law fit for Reuters-RCV1: b = 0.49 and k = 44.
results.setup: Least-squares fit of log10 M = 0.49 log10 T + 1.64 on Reuters-RCV1; fit is excellent for T > 10^5
results.note: The extracted text drops superscript formatting (T > 105 means 10^5).
results.quote: the fit is excellent for T > 105 = 100,000, for the parameter values b = 0.49 and k = 44.

results.claim: Heaps' law predicts 38,323 terms for the first 1,000,020 tokens; actual is 38,365.
results.setup: First 1,000,020 tokens of Reuters-RCV1, M = k T^b with k=44, b=0.49
results.note: Prediction 44 x 1,000,020^0.49 is printed as 38,323; the text writes the exponent expression as '1,000,0200.49'.
results.quote: The actual number is 38,365 terms, very close to the prediction.

results.claim: Typical Heaps' law parameters across collections.
results.setup: Generic ranges, no named collection
results.quote: Typical values for the parameters k and b are: 30 ≤k ≤100 and b ≈0.5.

results.claim: Case folding and stemming each reduce distinct terms by 17%.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1; case folding 473,723 to 391,523 terms; stemming (Porter) 391,373 to 322,383
results.quote: Stemming and case folding reduce the number of (distinct) terms by 17% each

results.claim: A 150-word stop list cuts 30% of nonpositional postings but the effect mostly vanishes after compression.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, reference line case folding: 96,969,056 to 67,001,847 postings; 94,516,599 tokens (-47%)
results.note: Text says 25% to 30% but the table gives -14% for 30 stop words and -30% for 150, so 25% fits neither row; 'a quarter or more' for 150 words is consistent with 30%.
results.quote: Eliminating the 150 most common words from indexing (as stop words; cf. Section 2.2.2, page 27) cuts 25% to 30% of the nonpositional
results.table: Table 5.1, row 150 stop words, column nonpositional postings delta %

results.claim: Rule of 30: the 30 most common words account for 30% of tokens in written text.
results.setup: Written text in general; the chapter says 31% in Table 5.1
results.note: Table 5.1 prints -31% tokens for 30 stop words against case folding, but 121,857,825 vs 179,158,204 is a 32.0% drop. Minor rounding difference.
results.quote: The rule of 30 states

results.claim: Gamma code is within a factor of 2 + 1/H(P) (at most 3) of the entropy bound for any distribution, so it is universal.
results.setup: Any distribution P with 1 < H(P) < infinity; proof referenced, not given
results.quote: γ encoding is within a factor of 3 of this optimal encoding, approaching 2 for large H(P):

results.claim: Gamma code length for gap G is 2 x floor(log2 G) + 1 bits.
results.setup: Elias gamma, gaps G >= 1
results.quote: so the length of the entire code is 2 × ⌊log2 G⌋+ 1 bits.

results.claim: Zipf-based model predicts a 224 MB gamma-coded postings file for Reuters-RCV1; the real one is 101 MB.
results.setup: Zipf law with c = 1/H_M ~ 1/13, Lc = 15, blocks of 15 terms, M/Lc ~ 27,000, uniform gaps within each term
results.note: Eq 5.7 prints the factor 2 × 10^6 x 15; with N = 800,000 documents the sum gives about 225 MB (I recomputed: 2N x 15 x sum_{j<=27000} log2 j / j = 224.99 MB), whereas 2 x 10^6 would give 281 MB. So the 10^6 is either a typo for 2N=1.6x10^6 or a rounded N. Also the unrounded model gives 251 MB (Table 4.2 numbers) and 254 MB on synthetic Zipf data.
results.quote: So the postings file of the compressed inverted index for our 960 MB collection has a size of 224 MB, one fourth the size of the original collection.

results.claim: Model discrepancy: the Zipf model predicts 251 MB and artificial Zipf-generated terms compress to 254 MB.
results.setup: Compressed index built from terms generated from the Zipf model
results.note: Text gives 251 MB for the unrounded model; Exercise 5.18 asks for 'about 251 MB'.
results.quote: then the compressed size is 254 MB.

results.claim: Ratio of compressed index plus dictionary to collection size with gamma and blocking with front coding is about 0.03.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1 with XML markup (3600 MB collection); (101 + 5.9)/3600
results.note: Against the 960 MB text-only collection the ratio is about 0.11; the caption itself says the XML markup makes the ratio especially small.

results.claim: Uncompressed 20-bit postings file is 250 MB for the 960 MB collection.
results.setup: Reuters-RCV1, 800,000 documents, 200 tokens per document, six characters per token, M=400,000 distinct terms, docID postings only (no frequencies or positions); docID = log2 800,000 ~ 20 bits; 100,000,000 postings
results.note: Table 5.1 case folding line has 96,969,056 postings; the chapter rounds to 100,000,000.

results.claim: Term incidence matrix for Reuters-RCV1 is 40 GB.
results.setup: 400,000 terms x 800,000 documents, one bit each

results.claim: Scholer et al.: VB codes process queries about two times faster than bit-level compressed or uncompressed indexes.
results.setup: Reported experiment; setup not given in chapter; VB has a 30% compression-ratio penalty against the best bit-level method
results.quote: variable byte codes process queries two times faster than either bit-level compressed indexes or uncompressed indexes with a 30% penalty in compression ratio

results.claim: Variable nibble codes compress 5% to 10% better than VB but cost up to one third in effectiveness.
results.setup: One experiment, setup not stated
results.quote: “variable nibble” codes showed 5% to 10% better compression

limits: Only docID postings are compressed; frequencies and positions are referred to Scholer et al. 2002 and Zobel and Moffat 2006 (p.86, p.106).
Only Boolean retrieval; for ranked retrieval the chapter says postings can be ordered by term frequency and notes weights should not be stored as they compress poorly (p.107).
All numbers are from one collection, Reuters-RCV1, which is mostly XML markup so ratios look especially small (Table 5.6 caption).
No timing numbers for decoding speed; the speed claims for VB versus gamma are qualitative or quoted from Scholer et al. 2002.
The Zipf model fit 'is not particularly good' (p.89) and the 224 MB estimate is more than double the real 101 MB.

Dated by 2008: no SIMD or frame-of-reference codes (PForDelta, SIMD-BP128, Elias-Fano, Roaring bitmaps), no dense vector indexes (HNSW, IVF-PQ) or learned sparse indexes; 32-bit pointers and 4 GB address spaces, disk seek costs and 'mobile phone' memory limits differ from today; web-scale docID widths are beyond 4 bytes as the chapter itself notes (p.91).
Word-aligned codes (Anh and Moffat 2005, 2006a; Zukowski et al. 2006) are named as faster and at least as efficient as VB but not described (p.106).
practices: Compress the dictionary so it fits in main memory, because disk seeks dominate query time (p.90).
Use variable byte codes for most IR systems as an excellent time-space tradeoff and simple to implement (p.98).
Use bit-level gamma or delta codes when disk space is scarce, accepting costlier decoding (p.98, p.103-104).
Store gaps between sorted docIDs instead of docIDs (p.96).
Use blocked dictionary storage with a moderate k, as large k makes lookup prohibitively slow (p.93).
Page a very large dictionary to disk and index the first term of each page with a B-tree (p.95).
Do not use minimal perfect hashing for the dictionary in a dynamic environment (p.95).
Do not precompute and store weights in the index; store frequencies as they compress better (p.107).
Assign docIDs so that similar documents are in a small range to make gaps small (p.106).

terms.definition: a docID in a postings list
estimates vocabulary size as a function of collection size: M = kT^b
the collection frequency of the ith most common term is proportional to 1/i
the 30 most common words account for 30% of the tokens in written text
lossless preserves all information; lossy discards some, e.g. case folding, stemming, stop word elimination
a common prefix is identified for a subsequence of the term list and then referred to with a special character
uses an integral number of bytes to encode a gap; last 7 bits are payload, first bit is a continuation bit set to 1 for the last byte
the unary code of n is a string of n 1s followed by a 0
splits a gap G into length (unary code of the offset length) and offset (G in binary with the leading 1 removed)
H(P) = -sum P(x) log2 P(x), a measure of uncertainty
a code with the property of being within a factor of optimal for an arbitrary distribution P
no code is the prefix of another, so decoding is unique without delimiters
a code that needs no fitted model parameters
like gamma code but encodes the length part in gamma code instead of unary
codes that explicitly model the probability distribution of gaps for each term

code.snippet:
VBENCODENUMBER(n)
1 bytes <- <>
2 while true
3 do PREPEND(bytes, n mod 128)
4 if n < 128
5 then BREAK
6 n <- n div 128
7 bytes[LENGTH(bytes)] += 128
8 return bytes
